stimulus.text:
J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur, Letters from an American Farmer, Letter III, “What Is an American?”, 1782:

“What then is the American, this new man? He is either an European, or the descendant of an European, hence that strange mixture of blood, which you will find in no other country. I could point out to you a family whose grandfather was an Englishman, whose wife was Dutch, whose son married a French woman, and whose present four sons have now four wives of different nations. He is an American, who leaving behind him all his ancient prejudices and manners, receives new ones from the new mode of life he has embraced, the new government he obeys, and the new rank he holds. ... Here individuals of all nations are melted into a new race of men, whose labours and posterity will one day cause great changes in the world. ... The American is a new man, who acts upon new principles; he must therefore entertain new ideas, and form new opinions.”
stimulus.source_note: J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur, Letters from an American Farmer (1782), Letter III. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus quoted verbatim from J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur, Letters from an American Farmer (1782), Letter III. Public domain.

primary_sources: J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur, Letters from an American Farmer (1782), Letter III

stem: A historian studying how Americans came to see themselves as a separate people would most likely use this passage as evidence of...

options.text: the belief that American laws came directly from English common law.
options.misconception: The passage is about a new people and new principles, not about English law.

options.text: the fact that most Americans in 1782 had been born in the United States.
options.misconception: The passage calls the American a European or the descendant of a European; it says nothing about where most Americans were born.

options.text: the idea that a distinct American character was forming after independence.
the decision to keep the British system of ranks and titles.
options.misconception: Background: the new republic rejected titles of nobility, and the passage describes a people without aristocratic families.

rationales.C: The passage defines the American as a new man with new principles, which is exactly a distinct character forming.
rationales.A: The passage never mentions English common law or any legal source.
rationales.B: The passage calls the American a European or the descendant of a European, not a native-born American.
rationales.D: The passage describes a new people, not a people keeping British ranks and titles.
rationales.general:
1. The passage calls the American a new man who acts upon new principles.
2. It says he forms new ideas and new opinions from his new mode of life.
3. Background: the passage was published in 1782, the year before the Treaty of Paris ended the war.
4. A historian can therefore use it to show a distinct American character forming after independence.
Remember: a source written during a change can show the change happening, not only the result.
